paras: The death of Will Davis followed a fight on September 1, 1903, at a railroad construction camp near Trussville, Jefferson County, Alabama, in which Davis, a Black laborer, was accused of killing W. G. "Waites" McCaa, a white paymaster, with an ax. Davis fled wounded while posses searched for him, and reports from Trussville said he would be lynched if caught. A Birmingham dispatch of September 7 said citizens had run him down and shot him to death, but after his decomposed body was found near Argo a week later, Birmingham and Montgomery papers said he had died of a wound from McCaa's brother.

McCaa, 24, of Birmingham, was paymaster for Brewer & Jones, contractors on the Seaboard Air Line's new work near Trussville, and his younger brother, B. B. McCaa, worked for the same firm. Davis, whom the Birmingham Age-Herald at first called Will Jones, worked around the firm's commissary and stables.

According to the Age-Herald, the trouble began on the afternoon of Tuesday, September 1, when McCaa ordered Davis to saddle his horse and found him slow and "impudent." McCaa then sent him for a hickory switch, reprimanded him, and, after Davis cursed him, drew his pistol and began beating him on the head with it. In the struggle McCaa's younger brother fired at Davis five times, by the Age-Herald's count; the Montgomery Advertiser said three or four shots "had no effect." McCaa was found dying of head wounds, which a physician attributed to blows from a blunt instrument; the papers said Davis used an ax.

Davis escaped, apparently wounded, and searchers followed a trail of blood, which one dispatch said ran for two miles. Coroner Paris of Birmingham led deputy sheriffs and armed citizens in the search, and the Age-Herald wrote that it was feared Davis "will be killed should he be caught." A wire report said several posses were after him and that he would be lynched if caught. By September 4 the Age-Herald doubted that the search would succeed.

On September 8 the Age-Herald carried a rumor that a searching party had killed the wounded man and hidden the body. A few days later a Black man brought to Birmingham from Smith Mines on suspicion of being Davis was released as "not the right negro."

On September 14 Davis's decomposed body was found in the woods at Argo, about five miles from Trussville; the Montgomery Advertiser said grape hunters found it. Coroner Paris identified the remains and, finding them too decomposed to handle, had them cremated. The Age-Herald then wrote that Davis had escaped with a wound from B. B. McCaa's shot and died at Argo, and the Advertiser said he died of gunshot wounds from McCaa's brother received in the fight. No report of an inquest finding on Davis's death, or of any arrest for it, appears in the coverage.

The coverage comes from white newspapers, led by the Birmingham Age-Herald, which followed the case in at least eight items between September 2 and 15. The Age-Herald and a Birmingham News report reprinted in the Montgomery Advertiser told the story from the McCaa side, under headlines such as "WAITES M'CAA WAS KILLED BY A NEGRO," and called Davis "surly" and "impudent."

Out of state, the Savannah Morning News ran the wire as "KILLED WITH AN AX," and the Americus Times-Recorder ran it as "NEGRO CRUSHED MAN'S SKULL," with the line that the man would be lynched if caught. The September 7 dispatch that Davis had been "run down and shot to death by citizens" appeared without comment as "McCaa's Murderer" in the Lexington, Mississippi, Progress-Advertiser on September 10 and in the Brookhaven Leader and Macon Beacon on September 12.

Accounts of Davis's death differ: the September 7 wire said citizens of a posse shot him after the brother's wound slowed him, while the Age-Herald a day later reported a killing by searchers only as rumor. After the body was found, both the Age-Herald and the Advertiser attributed his death to B. B. McCaa's shot, a version that came later and from the papers closest to the scene, though neither cited any examination of the cremated remains.

reader.title: Death of Will Davis
bases: A white paymaster was killed in a fight with a Black worker who fled wounded and was hunted by posses with threats of lynching (A2, A5); the one report that citizens shot him to death (A10) is contradicted by later local reports that he died of the brother's wound (A15, A16).

Davis died and was hunted by posses under threat of lynching (A2, A5), but only a Sept. 7 wire and its reprints say citizens shot him to death (A10, A12, A13), a claim the Age-Herald reported only as rumor (A8); after the body was found, the Birmingham and Montgomery papers said he died of B. B. McCaa's shot during or just after the fight (A15, A16), the later and more local evidence, though no examination of the cremated body was reported (A14).

The killing of McCaa, the flight and the manhunt are corroborated (A2, A3, A5), but how Davis died is reported three ways: shot by citizens (A10), rumored killed by searchers (A8), died of the brother's wound (A15, A16).

accounts.label: Birmingham Age-Herald local account (McCaa side)
accounts.gist: McCaa ordered Davis to saddle a horse, found him impudent, beat him with a pistol; Davis broke away, got the pistol, then killed McCaa with an ax while the brother fired five times.

accounts.label: Birmingham News special / wire
accounts.gist: A surly Davis quarreled with McCaa and killed him with an ax; the brother's three or four shots had no effect; posses out and lynching expected if caught.

accounts.label: Sept. 7 Birmingham wire
accounts.gist: Davis was run down and shot to death by citizens, the brother's wound having let the posse overtake him.

accounts.label: Local rumor
accounts.gist: A searching party found the wounded Davis and killed him, hiding the body.

accounts.label: Report after body found
accounts.gist: Davis escaped with the brother's bullet wound, got as far as Argo and died there of it.

framing.detail: The Age-Herald headlined 'WAITES M'CAA WAS KILLED BY A NEGRO' with a subhead 'Negro Impudent', and reported the fear that Davis would be killed if caught without comment.
Georgia papers ran 'KILLED WITH AN AX' and 'NEGRO CRUSHED MAN'S SKULL', the latter stating plainly that he would be lynched if caught.
Three Mississippi weeklies ran the 'McCaa's Murderer' item that Davis had been shot to death by citizens, with no comment.
